props.title: Walk Hard: The Dewey Cox Story
props.initialSlug: A rock legend's wild rise, told hilariously wrong

sections.content: Walk Hard: The Dewey Cox Story (2007) brilliantly skewers music biopics by amplifying their most ridiculous tropes. John C. Reilly's Dewey Cox parodies multiple musicians, but primarily channels Johnny Cash from Walk the Line (2005) and Ray Charles from Ray (2004). The film mercilessly mocks biopic clichés - the traumatic childhood, instant songwriting genius, drug spiral, redemption arc - while delivering genuinely catchy original songs. Director Jake Kasdan and writer Judd Apatow created not just a spoof, but a loving critique of how formulaic music biopics had become.

sections.content: The genius of Walk Hard lies in how it predicted and pre-emptively satirized the next decade of music biopics. Bohemian Rhapsody (2018) and Rocketman (2019) follow beat-for-beat many of the exact story points Walk Hard lampoons - from the "wrong kid died" childhood trauma to the "you don't want no part of this" drug scenes. The film even nails the way biopics compress time, with Dewey instantly mastering instruments and writing hit songs in single takes.

Beyond just spoofing musical biopics, Walk Hard stands as one of the best comedy films of its era. Like Airplane! (1980) and The Naked Gun (1988), it maintains a relentless pace of both broad slapstick and subtle background gags. The supporting cast, including Tim Meadows, Jenna Fischer, and Kristen Wiig, delivers perfectly straight-faced performances that sell the absurdity. The parade of musician cameos (Jack White as Elvis, Jack Black as Paul McCartney) adds another layer of meta-commentary. SUBHEAD: Musical Authenticity in Comedy

sections.content: What elevates Walk Hard above mere parody is the quality of its original music. Songs like "Walk Hard" and "Beautiful Ride" could genuinely work as straight country/rock songs, while "Let's Duet" and "Royal Jelly" perfectly capture the styles they're mimicking. This attention to musical detail follows in the tradition of A Mighty Wind (2003) and Music and Lyrics (2007), comedies that respect the genres they're sending up.
